The Complete AI Shorts Pipeline: Research, Production, Scale on $44 a Month

$277 a month. That is the bill for 11 AI providers at mid-tier plans, most sitting idle between projects. One model for images, another for video, another for audio, another for editing. Five subscriptions, twelve tabs, a folder full of assets nobody can trace back to the model that made them.
Meanwhile, the real bottleneck in AI short-form video was never generation speed. It was knowing which of the clips just generated is actually worth publishing, and which one only looks good because the creator spent ten minutes staring at it.
This guide covers the full pipeline that solves both problems: how to find formats already proven to hold attention, how to rebuild them through an orchestrated AI production stack, and how to scale the output without the process becoming the bottleneck. Total tool cost: $44 a month. The documented returns on this pipeline range from $12,900 in a single month to $20,000 across two weeks, depending on volume and monetization mix.
Bookmark this. The research prompt, the director brief, the automation logic, and the production architecture are all below.
The Pipeline
GPT-6 Astra  ->  Picsart  ->  Make

Research        Production    Scale
finds the       rebuilds     publishes,
proven format   it as yours  tracks, loops
1. Research: Find What Already Hit
GPT-6 Astra does the search. No extra cost, no extra tool.
Search for short-form videos posted in the last 14 days
in [your niche].

Find 10 clearly outperforming the channel's own average
(a channel that normally gets 20k views posting at 500k+).

For each one give me:
- the link
- the view count vs. channel's typical count
- the first 2 seconds, described in one line
- the format in one sentence, separated from the topic
  (topic = what it's about; format = the shape it's built in)

Rank by how easily the format reskins onto a different subject.
The critical output: one-sentence format description per video. That sentence is what moves to production. Not the video itself, not the topic -- the shape.
2. Production: Picsart as the Entire Stack
Why one platform instead of six. 11 AI providers at mid-tier plans run $277/month. Each handoff between them is a manual export and re-upload. By the fourth step nobody remembers which model produced the file being edited.
Picsart collapses this into two layers.
Playground → 188 models from 34 providers behind one prompt bar. Image, video, audio. One credit balance, cost shown on the button before generation runs. Assets save to Drive with metadata, open directly in the editor. No export, no re-upload.
Flow → visual no-code canvas. Models and assets connect as nodes. Work moves through stages: image generation, video, audio, edit, review, export. Step 5 can still see what step 1 produced. A rejection at step 6 does not discard the entire run.
AI Director Agent (Lina) → Picsart's agent marketplace includes a film director agent trained on the creator's output over time. This is where the research output enters production:
You are directing a 60-second short film.

Reference format: [one-line format from the research,
e.g. "countdown bottle short, one location, clock tension"].

My subject: [your footage, character, product — one line].

Break this into a scene-by-scene plan:
- number of scenes
- what happens in each, one line
- shot size and camera height per scene
- where the tone shifts, and what causes it
- the final beat that makes someone rewatch

Hold one visual rule across every scene and name it.
Never copy the reference's footage or characters. Only its shape.
Fix whatever made the reference weak: slow open, flat ending,
a beat that dragged. Name the fix as its own line.
The agent returns a director's plan on a proven shape, with the weak point already fixed. Each generated shot gets fed back before the next one is built. The agent checks it against its own plan and flags what breaks.
3. Automation: Make Closes the Loop
Trigger: new short lands in Google Drive folder

1. Read format tag from file name
2. Publish to TikTok, YouTube Shorts, Instagram Reels
3. Wait 48 hours, pull watch-through rate by format tag
4. Write completion rate into the research sheet
5. Flag any format beating the account median by 25%+
6. Telegram ping: which formats held this week
Setup: 2 hours once. The loop closes because the next research pass starts from what already worked.
The Volume Game
The output rate on this pipeline is 2 to 5 shorts per day. That changes the entire strategy. One format that holds attention, run as variations → same visual style, same character format, different hooks each time. Platforms reward consistency and frequency. A recognizable series beats unrelated one-offs for both watch-through and repeat viewers.
Revenue Breakdown
Platform payouts: $5,000-13,000/month. Formats rebuilt from proven templates start above the 20-30% completion floor. Volume does the rest.
Brand placements + retainer shorts: $2,500-5,500/month. $300-700 per short built on a proven format. Eight shorts a month on retainer.
Referral deals + pipeline sales: $2,000+/month. The pipeline itself -- research prompt plus director brief, tuned per niche -- sells as a kit with no per-sale labor.
Cost
Picsart Pro     $15/month
GPT-6 Astra     $20/month
Make Core        $9/month
Total            $44/month
The Point
Research finds what already hit. One orchestrated stack rebuilds it without losing the shape. Automation scales and feeds winners back into the next cycle.
Stop inventing. Start rebuilding.

hits.name: NO1ennn
hits.text:
this is f*cking gold

Google engineers built an agent that tests thousands of search strategies for the cost of running one, by letting it dream inside its own memory.

it is called Dream-RSI. Google, Google DeepMind, Maryland, Virginia. 17 authors.

the whole thing rests on one observation: a finished run is not a log. it is a map of a world that already exists.

> every discovery run records a tree. each node is one attempt with its full result stored
> that tree becomes a replay simulator. the paper calls them worlds 
> the agent dreams inside it: thousands of alternative strategies, testing different branches, different orders, different concurrency, different stopping rules
> every one of those evaluations costs zero execution. nothing is ever run twice
> the winner goes back online, produces a new tree, and the pool of worlds grows

the coding agent underneath is never touched. this is an orchestration layer sitting on top of whatever you already run.

what it bought them, against the same agent with a frozen strategy:

> Lasso: 3587ms down to 2931ms, on 317 agent calls instead of 550
> on Flash: 2517ms to 2351ms, 1879 calls instead of 3200
> both solvers beat sklearn and glmnet on all six held-out datasets
> GPU kernels: the same result on 2.43x and 1.79x fewer generations, then 2.09x and 1.44x better result on the same budget

one expensive run. thousands of free ones.

the model did not get smarter.
it got a memory it could rehearse in.

Anthropic scientist made a new cell biology discovery by pointing a loop at raw microscopy and letting it delete 317 of its own findings by morning.

It was never asked to identify anything. It was asked what would have to be true, and what would prove it wrong.

> WATCH - raw microscopy in, no labels, no prior dataset, no hint of what to look for
> NOTICE - marks only the frames that break pattern, ignores everything that fits
> PROPOSE - every idea leaves with its assumption stated, never as a bare claim
> KILL - discards anything no bench experiment could ever disprove
> QUEUE - what survives becomes a protocol a human can actually run in the morning

320 hypotheses went in. 3 came out. The 3 were not the most convincing ones.

They were the only ones that could fail, which is the entire filter and the entire point.

Everything else read like a finding. Plausible is free, and a hundred plausible results by morning is not a result, it is noise dressed up as progress.

One of the 3 survived nine consecutive nights and is now the discovery - a division timing shift nobody had a reason to look for, confirmed on a bench by someone who knew nothing about it a week ago.

A lab pays a postdoc a full year to narrow a question that far. This narrowed it between midnight and breakfast, for the cost of the electricity.

Nobody deletes their own good-looking output. That is why the kill gate is a separate seat and not a preference the model can override.

How it's wired is in the article below.
